catalog_quote: 2.3. Stress In Waimiri Atroari, stress is not a contrastive feature. In bisyllabic words, stress falls on the final position syllable. Words with more than two syllables may possibly have primary and secondary stress. Syllable with long vowels and glottalized vowels are stressed. (34) (a) kaá.pa 'garden' (d) ka.pá 'she/he talked' (b) my.dý 'house' (e) wu.ré 'fan' (c) ta.bé'e 'capybara' (f) ty.rý.ny 'any small bird'

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the deciding passage is verbatim at sec. 2.3, printed p. 94 of the open-access PDF we hold. The source is a 2010 phonology article by the language's main linguist, restating her 2003 dissertation, so the classification (non-contrastive stress; final in disyllables; CVV/glottalized syllables attract stress; polysyllables hedged -> weight-sensitive (tentative), weight class CVV, edge unclear) faithfully reflects what the best-placed author published, and no other prosody study exists per Crossref/Glottolog. It is 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced' because the deciding text is a four-sentence summary while a 185-pp grammar by the same author (Bruno 2003) and a 46-pp phonological sketch (Hill & Hill) exist and are not yet obtained; the dissertation could resolve the hedge on 3+ syllable words (e.g. to a stated default position plus weight), which would refine edge/kind but is unlikely to contradict the wei
